hist.ancient.greece.athens-thought-elect.title: Athens thought elections were the aristocratic option
hist.ancient.greece.athens-thought-elect.hook: Classical Athens used elections only where it had to. The democratic method was the lottery.
hist.ancient.greece.athens-thought-elect.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Dated the kleroterion to the fourth century BCE, attributed the lot-vs-election reasoning to Aristotle (Politics 1294b) as received opinion, added that source, cross-linked the democracy series.

hist.ancient.greece.athens-thought-elect.body: Most Athenian public posts were filled by lot. The Boule of five hundred was drawn each year; from the fourth century BCE juries were allotted on the morning of the trial by a slotted stone machine, the *kleroterion*, built specifically to make rigging hard. Voting was kept for jobs where competence obviously mattered, such as the ten generals. Aristotle records the received view — lot is democratic, election oligarchic — because elections favour the famous and the rich, and a lottery cannot be canvassed.

recall.question: Which Athenian offices were elected rather than allotted, and why?
recall.answer: Mainly military ones, above all the ten generals, on the view that they needed proven skill. Everything else went to the lot, because election was seen as favouring wealth and reputation.

hist.ancient.mesopotamia-writing.receipt.title: Writing was invented to settle accounts
hist.ancient.mesopotamia-writing.receipt.hook: The oldest writing in the world is not a poem or a prayer. It is a list of how much barley somebody owed.
hist.ancient.mesopotamia-writing.receipt.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Schmandt-Besserat's token-to-writing reconstruction relabelled 'widely contested' rather than 'debated'.

hist.ancient.mesopotamia-writing.receipt.body: The earliest tablets from Uruk, roughly 3300 BCE, carry no gods and no kings. They carry quantities: barley, beer, sheep, textiles, and the names of whoever was owed them. Literature turns up centuries later. Denise Schmandt-Besserat traced the signs back further, to clay tokens sealed inside clay envelopes — accounting that existed before writing did, though her reconstruction is widely contested. Humanity learned to write because it could not remember who owed what.

recall.question: What kind of text dominates the earliest cuneiform tablets?
recall.answer: Administrative accounts — rations, debts and deliveries of barley, beer and livestock. Narrative and religious texts appear only centuries afterwards.

hist.economic.bretton-woods.keynes-lost-.title: The plan that lost at Bretton Woods
hist.economic.bretton-woods.keynes-lost-.hook: Keynes went to Bretton Woods with a plan to punish surplus countries too. He lost, and the losing plan explains the next thirty years.
hist.economic.bretton-woods.keynes-lost-.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Triffin put the dilemma to Congress on 28 October 1959, not in 1960; Gold and the Dollar Crisis is the 1960 book. Dilemma heading re-dated.

hist.economic.bretton-woods.keynes-lost-.body:
From 1 to 22 July 1944, with the war still running, 730 delegates from 44 nations met at a hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to design the monetary system of a world that did not exist yet.

Two plans were on the table. John Maynard Keynes proposed an International Clearing Union with its own unit of account, the *bancor*, and one radical feature: it charged countries that ran persistent surpluses as well as those that ran deficits. If Germany sells far more than it buys, someone else must be borrowing to buy it, and Keynes wanted the adjustment shared. Harry Dexter White, for the United States, proposed a fund where deficit countries adjust and surplus countries accumulate as they please.

The United States held the gold and the creditor position, so White won. The result was the IMF, the World Bank, currencies pegged to a dollar pegged to gold, and an asymmetry that has never gone away.

The trouble with the winning plan was visible before it collapsed.
hist.economic.bretton-woods.keynes-lost-.rigor:
Two constraints explain both the system and its end.

**The trilemma.** A country cannot simultaneously have a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility and an independent monetary policy; it must pick two. Bretton Woods chose the fixed rate and monetary independence, and paid for them with capital controls — which is why the era looks so orderly, and why liberalising capital in the 1960s destabilised it.

**The Triffin dilemma.** If one country's currency is the world's reserve asset, the world's demand for reserves grows with world trade. The issuer can only supply them by running balance-of-payments deficits. But the more dollars are held abroad relative to the gold backing them, the less credible convertibility at $\$35$ per ounce becomes. Supply the world and lose credibility; protect credibility and starve the world of liquidity. Robert Triffin put this to Congress on 28 October 1959, and to everyone else in *Gold and the Dollar Crisis* the year after.

Both ends duly arrived. On 15 August 1971 Nixon suspended convertibility, and by 1973 the major currencies floated. Keynes's bancor was an attempt to dodge Triffin by making the reserve asset belong to no one — which is roughly what the IMF's Special Drawing Rights, created in 1969, tried and mostly failed to be.

options.text: That fixed exchange rates always collapse under speculative attack
options.why: attacks are a symptom; Triffin's point is about reserve supply.

options.text: Supplying the world with reserves requires the issuer to run deficits
options.why: and those same deficits undermine confidence in convertibility.

options.text: That surplus countries face no pressure to adjust
options.why: true of the White plan, and Keynes's complaint, but a different problem.

hist.economic.hyperinflations.prices-dou.title: Remember what money is? Hungary, 1946, says it again
hist.economic.hyperinflations.prices-dou.hook: In Hungary in 1946 prices doubled about every fifteen hours. What is money, if it can do that?
hist.economic.hyperinflations.prices-dou.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Callback opening now names hyperinflation. Sargent's four inflations dated to the 1920s (they exclude Hungary 1946). Unsourced street-sweeping detail replaced with the photographed one.

hist.economic.hyperinflations.prices-dou.body:
Hyperinflation has a record holder, and it is Hungary after the war: by July 1946 prices were doubling roughly every fifteen hours. The largest note actually issued was 100 million *b.-pengő*, which is a 1 followed by twenty zeros; a note for ten times more was printed and never released. On 1 August 1946 the forint replaced the pengő at a rate of 400 octillion to one. Photographs from January 1946 show banknotes left lying uncollected on the Danube bank.

This is the cleanest demonstration of what money is. Not a substance. A shared bet that somebody else will accept the thing tomorrow. Once the bet fails, people spend faster, the same notes chase goods more often, and prices climb faster than the printing — which is why hyperinflations accelerate instead of settling.

The ending is the part worth carrying. Hyperinflations do not fade out; they stop, often within days. Thomas Sargent's study of four 1920s cases argued the common ingredient is not slow monetary tightening but a credible change of fiscal regime: the government visibly stops needing the printing press. Expectations, not the money stock alone, are what break.

recall.question: According to Sargent's account of the classic hyperinflations, what actually ended them?

options.text: A gradual reduction in the growth rate of the money supply
options.why: the endings were abrupt, not gradual.

options.text: A credible, visible change of fiscal regime that removed the government's need to print
options.why: after which expectations, and prices, stabilised quickly.

options.text: Price controls and rationing
options.why: these were tried in several cases and did not stop the inflation.

sources.title: The Ends of Four Big Inflations
sources.author: Thomas J. Sargent

hist.latam.colombia.como-se-perdio-panam.title: Cómo se perdió Panamá
hist.latam.colombia.como-se-perdio-panam.hook: El Senado colombiano rechazó el tratado del canal en agosto de 1903 para negociar mejor. En noviembre ya no había nada que negociar.
hist.latam.colombia.como-se-perdio-panam.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Added exact Urrutia-Thomson dates (firmado 6 abr 1914, ratificado 20 abr 1921). Kept 'agosto de 1903' for the Senate rejection: sources split between 12 and 18 August.

hist.latam.colombia.como-se-perdio-panam.body:
El 22 de enero de 1903 se firmó el tratado Herrán-Hay: diez millones de dólares de contado, doscientos cincuenta mil anuales, y un arriendo renovable de cien años sobre una franja de seis millas a través del istmo. El Senado de Estados Unidos lo ratificó en marzo.

El Senado colombiano lo rechazó en agosto. Las razones no eran absurdas: soberanía, y el cálculo de que si se esperaba a que expirara la concesión de la compañía francesa, Colombia podría cobrar mucho más. El país venía de la Guerra de los Mil Días, con el tesoro vacío y el gobierno débil.

El 3 de noviembre Panamá se declaró independiente. El USS *Nashville* estaba en el puerto e impidió que las tropas colombianas se movieran por el ferrocarril. El 18 de noviembre Washington firmó el tratado del canal con Philippe Bunau-Varilla, ingeniero francés y representante del flamante país.

La factura llegó tarde: el tratado Urrutia-Thomson, firmado el 6 de abril de 1914, le pagó a Colombia veinticinco millones de dólares. El Senado estadounidense lo ratificó el 20 de abril de 1921, cuando ya había petróleo colombiano de por medio.

recall.question: ¿Por qué rechazó el Senado colombiano el tratado Herrán-Hay en 1903?

options.text: Porque Colombia no quería un canal en su territorio
options.why: el canal se buscaba desde hacía décadas.

options.text: Por soberanía y por dinero
options.why: esperar a que expirara la concesión francesa prometía un pago mucho mayor, y el arriendo se veía como cesión de territorio.

options.text: Porque prefería la ruta por Nicaragua
options.why: esa era una opción discutida en Washington, no la razón del rechazo en Bogotá.

hist.latam.colombia.la-hora-gaviria.title: El día que Colombia cambió de hora y nadie se lo devolvió
hist.latam.colombia.la-hora-gaviria.hook: En 1992 Colombia adelantó los relojes una hora para ahorrar luz. Fue la única vez que el país tuvo horario de verano.
hist.latam.colombia.la-hora-gaviria.author: lead
hist.latam.colombia.la-hora-gaviria.body:
El 2 de marzo de 1992 el gobierno de César Gaviria anunció cortes de luz. El fenómeno de El Niño había secado los embalses de un sistema eléctrico casi todo hidráulico, y en Bogotá el racionamiento llegó a nueve horas diarias; en San Andrés, a dieciocho.

Entre las medidas hubo una rarísima: a la medianoche del 2 de mayo de 1992 el país adelantó los relojes de UTC−5 a UTC−4 para aprovechar la luz del sol. La llamaron «hora Gaviria». Duró unos nueve meses y el racionamiento terminó el 7 de febrero de 1993. Es la única vez que Colombia ha usado horario de verano: tan cerca del ecuador, el día casi no se mueve, y el ahorro no apareció.

Lo interesante no es el apagón sino lo que dejó. Las leyes 142 y 143 de 1994 desagruparon generación, transmisión, distribución y comercialización, y crearon el mercado mayorista. Más adelante llegó el «cargo por confiabilidad», que le paga a quien garantice energía cuando no llueve. Las instituciones se diseñan cuando duele.

recall.question: ¿Qué problema de incentivos dejó al descubierto el apagón de 1992?
recall.answer: Que nadie estaba pagando por tener capacidad disponible para la sequía. El mercado mayorista de 1994 y, más tarde, el cargo por confiabilidad existen para ponerle precio a esa garantía.

hist.latam.colombia.la-una-y-cinco-de-la.title: La una y cinco de la tarde, carrera séptima
hist.latam.colombia.la-una-y-cinco-de-la.hook: Gaitán salía a almorzar. Le dispararon en plena carrera séptima y Bogotá ardió tres días.
hist.latam.colombia.la-una-y-cinco-de-la.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Dropped the unsourced 'tres tiros'; added the Banrepcultural source that confirms 1:05 p.m.; death estimate tightened to 500-3.000.

hist.latam.colombia.la-una-y-cinco-de-la.body:
El 9 de abril de 1948 Jorge Eliécer Gaitán salió de su oficina en el edificio Agustín Nieto a almorzar. Juan Roa Sierra le disparó en plena carrera séptima. La multitud lo linchó ahí mismo y arrastró el cuerpo hasta el palacio presidencial, de modo que la única persona que podía explicar el crimen murió media hora después que la víctima.

Bogotá ardió tres días. Las estimaciones de muertos van de 500 a 3.000, según quién cuente. En la ciudad sesionaba la IX Conferencia Panamericana, la que creó la OEA, y por ahí andaba un estudiante cubano de veintiún años llamado Fidel Castro.

El magnicidio no inventó la violencia partidista: ya venía desde 1946. Le puso fecha, nombre y un país entero de testigos.

recall.question: ¿Por qué nunca se aclaró quién ordenó el asesinato de Gaitán?
recall.answer: Porque la multitud linchó a Juan Roa Sierra en el acto. El único testigo capaz de decir si actuó solo o por encargo murió el mismo 9 de abril, y todas las hipótesis posteriores son reconstrucciones indirectas.

hist.latam.colombian-conflict.una-guerra.title: Una guerra sin nombre propio
hist.latam.colombian-conflict.una-guerra.hook: Murieron alrededor de doscientas mil personas y el país nunca le puso un nombre propio: le dice La Violencia, como si fuera el clima.
hist.latam.colombian-conflict.una-guerra.author: author-humanities-1
hist.latam.colombian-conflict.una-guerra.body:
Las demás guerras tienen nombre: la de los Mil Días, la de Corea, la del Chaco. Esta se llama La Violencia, un sustantivo común, como si hubiera sido una temporada de lluvias.

Las cifras explican por qué costó nombrarla. Las estimaciones de muertos entre 1948 y 1958 van de 113.000 a 300.000, y la cifra que más se repite es doscientos mil; más de dos millones de personas salieron del campo. Pero no hubo frentes, ni ejércitos uniformados, ni batallas con fecha. Hubo veredas donde los liberales mataron conservadores y veredas donde pasó al revés, con la identidad partidista heredada del abuelo funcionando como bando.

Ese es el rasgo difícil de digerir: la guerra se peleó entre vecinos, por una etiqueta política que casi nadie había elegido. El asesinato de Gaitán en abril de 1948 la aceleró, no la inició.

Y terminó de una manera igual de particular: no la ganó nadie. Los dos partidos pactaron repartirse el poder durante dieciséis años, y el conteo de muertos se desplomó.

recall.question: ¿Qué distingue a La Violencia de una guerra civil convencional?

options.text: Que enfrentó al Estado contra una guerrilla organizada
options.why: eso describe mejor el conflicto posterior a 1964.

options.text: Que fue local y entre vecinos
options.why: sin frentes ni ejércitos regulares, con la filiación partidista heredada haciendo de bando.

options.text: Que fue una guerra urbana
options.why: el grueso de los muertos y del desplazamiento fue rural.

hist.latam.economic-history.prebisch-y-l.title: ¿Te acuerdas de los términos de intercambio? Prebisch los volvió política
hist.latam.economic-history.prebisch-y-l.hook: Si exportas café e importas maquinaria, y el café se abarata frente a la maquinaria, trabajas más cada año por lo mismo.
hist.latam.economic-history.prebisch-y-l.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: 'una razon inocente' changed to 'un cociente inocente' (razon reads ambiguously in Spanish).

hist.latam.economic-history.prebisch-y-l.body:
La idea de términos de intercambio suele aparecer como un cociente inocente: cuántas importaciones compra una unidad de exportación. Raúl Prebisch, un argentino que dirigió la CEPAL entre 1950 y 1963, la usó para reescribir cómo se veía la región.

Su informe de 1949, *El desarrollo económico de la América Latina y algunos de sus principales problemas*, propuso un mundo partido en **centro** y **periferia**: el centro produce manufacturas y tecnología, la periferia produce materias primas, y el precio relativo de lo que vende la periferia baja con el tiempo. Si eso es cierto, exportar más café no es un camino al desarrollo, es una caminadora.

De ahí salió la receta que definió treinta años de política económica en América Latina: industrialización por sustitución de importaciones, aranceles, bancos de fomento. Colombia la aplicó en serio desde los años cincuenta.
hist.latam.economic-history.prebisch-y-l.rigor:
La hipótesis Prebisch-Singer, formulada por separado en 1949 y 1950, dice que el precio relativo de los productos primarios frente a las manufacturas tiene tendencia negativa de largo plazo. El mecanismo propuesto tiene dos piezas:

1. **Elasticidad ingreso de la demanda.** Por la ley de Engel, la demanda de alimentos y materias primas crece menos que proporcionalmente con el ingreso mundial; la de manufacturas, más. Si el ingreso mundial crece a tasa $g$ y las elasticidades son $\eta_P < 1 < \eta_M$, la demanda relativa de lo primario cae de forma sostenida.
2. **Asimetría institucional.** En el centro, sindicatos y oligopolios convierten las ganancias de productividad en salarios y márgenes; en la periferia, con mercados laborales excedentarios y competencia atomizada, las ganancias de productividad se trasladan al precio, es decir, se le regalan al comprador.

La evidencia es más débil que la retórica. Las series largas de precios construidas después encuentran una tendencia negativa real pero pequeña, muy sensible al índice de manufacturas que se use y a dónde se pongan los quiebres estructurales, y los auges de materias primas de los años setenta y dos mil se ven mal desde la hipótesis. El balance de la sustitución de importaciones tampoco es limpio: industria sí, productividad y exportaciones mucho menos.

recall.question: ¿Cuál es el mecanismo que Prebisch y Singer proponen para el deterioro de los términos de intercambio?

options.text: Que los países periféricos producen con menos tecnología
options.why: la brecha tecnológica es parte del cuadro, pero no es el mecanismo del deterioro.

options.text: Demanda e instituciones
options.why: la demanda de materias primas crece menos que el ingreso, y en la periferia la mayor productividad baja precios en vez de subir salarios.

options.text: Que la moneda de la periferia se deprecia
options.why: la depreciación afecta precios nominales, no la tendencia de los precios relativos.

sources.title: Comisión Económica para América Latina y el Caribe

hist.latam.independence.carta-de-jamaica.title: «Una sola nación con un solo vínculo»
hist.latam.independence.carta-de-jamaica.hook: Derrotado y sin ejército, en Kingston, Bolívar escribe la idea más ambiciosa del continente y explica por qué no va a ocurrir.
hist.latam.independence.carta-de-jamaica.author: author-humanities-1
hist.latam.independence.carta-de-jamaica.body:
> «Es una idea grandiosa pretender formar de todo el Mundo Nuevo una sola nación con un solo vínculo que ligue sus partes entre sí y con el todo.»

Simón Bolívar, Carta de Jamaica, Kingston, 6 de septiembre de 1815, escrita derrotado y sin ejército.

Lo notable es lo que sigue: él mismo concluye que no es posible, por las distancias, los climas y los intereses opuestos. El sueño y su refutación en la misma página, quince años antes de que la Gran Colombia se deshiciera.

hist.latam.independence.el-20-de-julio-n.title: El 20 de julio no fue lo que celebramos
hist.latam.independence.el-20-de-julio-n.hook: El 20 de julio de 1810 Santa Fe no declaró la independencia. Juró lealtad a Fernando VII.
hist.latam.independence.el-20-de-julio-n.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Removed the unverified attribution of the florero request to Luis de Rubio; the cited source names Santamaria and the Morales brothers.

hist.latam.independence.el-20-de-julio-n.body:
El altercado del florero fue planeado. Antonio Morales propuso provocar al comerciante español José González Llorente, y esa mañana un grupo fue a pedirle prestado un florero sabiendo que diría que no. Dijo que no. La plaza se llenó.

Y lo que salió de ahí, el acta del cabildo extraordinario de ese 20 de julio de 1810, crea una Junta Suprema de Gobierno **en nombre de Fernando VII**, el rey preso de Napoleón. No es una declaración de independencia: es una junta, como las que se armaron en media América y en la propia España, para gobernar mientras el rey no estaba.

La independencia de verdad tardó nueve años más y fue una guerra. Entre 1810 y 1816 las provincias se pelearon entre ellas —la Patria Boba— y Pablo Morillo reconquistó el virreinato. El 7 de agosto de 1819, en el puente de Boyacá, dos horas de combate dejaron 13 muertos patriotas y unos 1.600 prisioneros realistas. Tres días después Bolívar entró a Santafé sin disparar.

recall.question: ¿Qué estableció el acta del 20 de julio de 1810 en Santa Fe?

options.text: La independencia absoluta de España
options.why: eso llegó años después, y por la vía militar.

options.text: Una Junta Suprema de Gobierno en nombre de Fernando VII
options.why: autonomía sí, ruptura con la corona todavía no.

options.text: La creación de la Gran Colombia
options.why: la Gran Colombia se funda en Angostura en 1819.

sources.title: Acta del Cabildo Extraordinario de Santa Fe de 1810

hist.latam.nation-building.bolivar-y-san.title: Dos hombres, dos ideas de país
hist.latam.nation-building.bolivar-y-san.hook: El héroe y su vicepresidente se volvieron enemigos por una pregunta que Colombia todavía no cierra: cuánto poder debe tener el ejecutivo.
hist.latam.nation-building.bolivar-y-san.author: author-humanities-1
hist.latam.nation-building.bolivar-y-san.body:
Ganada la guerra, quedó la pregunta difícil: cómo se gobierna esto. Bolívar quería un ejecutivo fuerte sobre un territorio enorme y recién armado; en su proyecto de constitución para Bolivia, de 1826, llegó a proponer una presidencia vitalicia. Santander, que quedó de vicepresidente de la Gran Colombia desde el Congreso de Cúcuta de 1821 y gobernó Bogotá mientras Bolívar hacía campaña en el sur, defendía la ley escrita, el congreso y las cuentas.

La pelea no era de egos, aunque también. Era una discusión de diseño institucional bajo estrés: guerra sin plata, provincias sin caminos, y un ejército al que había que pagarle.

Se rompió en 1828. Fracasó la Convención de Ocaña, Bolívar se declaró dictador y el 25 de septiembre un grupo entró al palacio a matarlo. Santander fue condenado a muerte por conspiración, y Bolívar le conmutó la pena por destierro. La Gran Colombia se disolvió en 1830.

Lo que quedó es el péndulo: federalismo en 1863, centralismo en 1886, descentralización en 1991. La misma pregunta, otra vez.

recall.question: ¿Cuál era el fondo institucional del enfrentamiento entre Bolívar y Santander?

options.text: Si Colombia debía seguir siendo colonia española
options.why: ninguno de los dos discutía eso en 1828.

options.text: Cuánto poder concentrar en el ejecutivo frente al congreso y las provincias
options.why: Bolívar por el mando fuerte, Santander por la ley y el control legislativo.

options.text: Si abolir o no la esclavitud
options.why: hubo debate sobre eso, pero no es lo que rompe la Gran Colombia.

hist.latam.precolumbian.el-dorado-era-un.title: El Dorado era una persona, no un lugar
hist.latam.precolumbian.el-dorado-era-un.hook: El Dorado no era una ciudad ni un reino. Era un hombre cubierto de polvo de oro, una vez, en una laguna.
hist.latam.precolumbian.el-dorado-era-un.author: author-humanities-1
hist.latam.precolumbian.el-dorado-era-un.body:
En el altiplano cundiboyacense, los muiscas hacían una ceremonia en la laguna de Guatavita: al heredero del cacique lo cubrían el cuerpo con polvo de oro, lo llevaban en una balsa hasta el centro del agua y allí ofrendaba oro y esmeraldas. El dorado era él.

De ahí salió todo lo demás. Sebastián de Belalcázar oyó de un indígena la historia de un señor que se untaba de oro, y los europeos hicieron con ella lo que hacen las expectativas sin evidencia: el hombre se volvió una ciudad, la ciudad se volvió un reino, y gente entera se murió buscándolo en el Orinoco y en la Guayana.

Conviene ser honesto con la fuente. La descripción más citada de la ceremonia la escribió Juan Rodríguez Freyle en *El Carnero*, entre 1636 y 1638, más de un siglo después de la conquista y de oídas. Lo que no es de oídas es la balsa muisca: una pieza de oro con la escena completa, hallada en 1969 en una cueva en Pasca y hoy en el Museo del Oro.

recall.question: ¿A qué se refería originalmente el nombre «el dorado»?
recall.answer: A una persona: el heredero del cacique de Guatavita, cubierto de polvo de oro para la ceremonia en la laguna. La ciudad y el reino dorados son una invención europea posterior.

hist.medieval.black-death.the-plague-tra.title: Remember that contagion follows edges, not distance?
hist.medieval.black-death.the-plague-tra.hook: Remember that epidemics spread along networks, not across maps? Here is the fourteenth century proving it.
hist.medieval.black-death.the-plague-tra.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected the 1347-48 chronology (Genoa/Marseille that winter, Tunis by April 1348). The Caffa catapult story is uncorroborated (de' Mussi, not an eyewitness), not 'treated with caution'.

hist.medieval.black-death.the-plague-tra.body:
When you met contagion on networks, the punchline was that the map is a bad predictor. What matters is who is connected to whom, and one long-range edge can drop an outbreak into a fresh population geography would have protected for months.

The Black Death is that model drawn in blood. It did not creep outward from a point; it rode the Genoese and Venetian shipping lanes: from the Black Sea, where it broke out during the siege of Caffa in 1346, to Messina in October 1347, then Genoa and Marseille over the winter of 1347–48, and Tunis by April 1348. Ports fell first and hard; inland districts a week's cart ride from a harbour often had months of grace, and a few mountain valleys were barely touched. Distance from the outbreak predicts little. Distance along the trade graph predicts a lot.

The story attached to Caffa — besiegers catapulting plague corpses over the walls — rests on a single late chronicle by Gabriele de' Mussi, who was not there: uncorroborated rather than refuted. The network, though, is not legend: Europe's commercial connectivity, its great fourteenth-century asset, was also its delivery system.
hist.medieval.black-death.the-plague-tra.rigor:
A contagion on a graph is governed by the contact structure, not by Euclidean position. In the simplest branching approximation, an outbreak grows while the basic reproduction number $R_0 > 1$, and on a network with degree distribution $p_k$ the relevant quantity is the mean excess degree,

$$\kappa = \frac{\langle k^2 \rangle}{\langle k \rangle},$$

so hubs — the ports — dominate both the speed and the probability of takeoff. Medieval Europe's trade graph is exactly the heavy-tailed, small-world case: a few enormously connected harbours, many weakly connected villages, and occasional long edges that make the effective diameter small.

That is why the honest historical claim is conditional. Mortality in 1348 correlates with commercial connectivity far better than with distance from the Black Sea, and the same structure explains why plague kept returning: reintroduction along the same edges, not persistence in place.

One caveat worth carrying: the *transmission* mechanism inside a town — rat fleas, human ectoparasites, or person-to-person in pneumonic form — is still argued over, and it changes the local dynamics without changing the network story at all.

recall.question: Why did some inland regions escape the worst of 1348 while distant ports were devastated?

options.text: Inland populations had partial immunity
options.why: no evidence supports prior immunity in 1347.

options.text: Transmission followed trade connections
options.why: a well-connected harbour was effectively closer to the outbreak than a nearby inland valley.

options.text: Colder inland climates killed the bacterium
options.why: plague struck cold regions, including Norway, severely.

hist.medieval.black-death.the-wages-that.title: The wages that would not stay down
hist.medieval.black-death.the-wages-that.hook: The clearest evidence that wages rose after the plague is the law passed to stop them.
hist.medieval.black-death.the-wages-that.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: England 7m to 2m was wrong (Broadberry: 4.8m in 1348 to 2.1m in 1400). 'Nominal wages doubled 1350-1450' was false (Clark: +19%) - rigor rebuilt on Clark and Munro. 1381 trigger fixed.

hist.medieval.black-death.the-wages-that.body:
Between 1347 and 1351 somewhere between a third and sixty per cent of Europe died, wildly unevenly by region. England went from about 4.8 million people in 1348 to about 2.1 million by 1400. Whole villages were abandoned.

The survivors inherited an economy with the same fields, the same ploughs, the same mills and far fewer hands. Labour became scarce and therefore expensive, and tenants who could walk to a better manor did. Landlords reacted the way people with political power react: England issued the Ordinance of Labourers in 1349 and the Statute of Labourers in 1351, forbidding any worker to demand more than the wages of 1346.

That law is the good evidence. Nobody legislates against a wage rise that is not happening. The statutes were enforced and resented for thirty years, a standing grievance behind the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 — though what actually lit that was the poll tax.

Whether the gains lasted, and how they diverged, is where historians stop agreeing.
hist.medieval.black-death.the-wages-that.rigor:
Two claims need separating, and the popular version blurs them. **Nominal** wages jumped at once, 1348 to 1350, and then crawled: Gregory Clark's series has English farm labour at 3.08d a day in 1350 and 3.66d in 1450, under twenty per cent across a century. The bigger move is in **real** wages, which John Munro's estimates put at roughly two to three times their pre-plague level by the mid-fifteenth century — because grain prices fell while money wages held.

The deeper dispute, from the Brenner debate of the 1970s onward, is about why the same shock produced opposite institutions. Western Europe saw serfdom decay into cash rents and copyhold tenure; eastern Europe saw lords tighten the law and bind peasants harder, the so-called second serfdom. Identical demographic shock, opposite outcome, so demography alone cannot be the explanation. Brenner's answer was the prior balance of class power and the density of peasant organisation; his critics point to land-labour ratios, urbanisation and the market for grain.

The honest summary: the Black Death is the best natural experiment in pre-modern economic history, and it does not identify a single effect. It identifies an interaction between a shock and whatever institutions were standing when it hit.

recall.question: Why do historians read the Statute of Labourers of 1351 as evidence about wages?

options.text: It caps wages at pre-plague 1346 levels
options.why: a law like that is only written when wages are actually rising.

options.text: It records the wages that were paid
options.why: it prescribes a maximum, and the enforcement records show it was widely broken.

options.text: It was the first English wage law
options.why: earlier wage regulation existed; what is new is the post-plague pressure behind it.

hist.medieval.mongols.the-message-never-.title: The message never got tired, only the horses did
hist.medieval.mongols.the-message-never-.hook: The Mongol post moved at the speed of a fresh horse, never a tired one.
hist.medieval.mongols.the-message-never-.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Spacing and speed were misattributed: ~25 miles and 200-250 miles a day are Marco Polo's figures, not 'the chroniclers''. Polo added as a source; diagram and recall relabelled.

hist.medieval.mongols.the-message-never-.body: Across the Mongol empire stood relay stations, the *yam*, about twenty-five miles apart by Marco Polo's count. A courier carrying a *paiza*, an engraved tablet of authority, swapped his spent horse for a rested one at each station and rode on. Polo claims express riders made two hundred to two hundred and fifty miles in a day. That is a traveller's number, not a ledger's, so read it as an order of magnitude. The idea, though, is exact: the empire's news outran its armies.

recall.question: What is the trick that let a Mongol dispatch sustain a speed no single rider could?
recall.answer: Only the horse is relieved, not the message. Relay stations roughly every twenty-five miles supplied a fresh mount, so the dispatch travelled at gallop pace continuously instead of decaying to the endurance of one animal.

sources.title: The Travels of Marco Polo, Book II
sources.author: Marco Polo

hist.modern.globalization.the-metal-box.title: A trucker got bored waiting at the docks
hist.modern.globalization.the-metal-box.hook: The single object that did most for globalisation is a corrugated steel box with no moving parts.
hist.modern.globalization.the-metal-box.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Levinson's figures are $5.83 a ton against 15.8 cents, not $5.86 and 16 cents; corrected in body and recall. McLean's dock epiphany labelled possibly apocryphal, as Levinson does.

hist.modern.globalization.the-metal-box.body:
Malcom McLean ran a trucking company in North Carolina. The story he told was of sitting in a queue at a Hoboken pier in 1937, watching longshoremen move his cargo one sack at a time, and wondering why the whole trailer could not simply be lifted aboard. Marc Levinson, who wrote the book on this, calls that origin story possibly apocryphal.

On 26 April 1956 a converted tanker, the *Ideal-X*, left Newark for Houston carrying 58 metal boxes on its deck. Loading a ship by hand cost about \$5.83 a ton at the time. With containers it cost 15.8 cents. That is not an improvement; it is a different industry.

Everything downstream followed: cranes, standard sizes, ports moving from crowded city waterfronts to open land, dockworker unions gutted, and the cost of distance falling far enough that manufacturing could be split across oceans. Nothing was invented that a nineteenth-century engineer could not have built. The hard part was getting railways, truckers, ports and unions to agree on a box.

recall.question: Why is the container usually credited with more than the ships that carry it?
recall.answer: Because the binding cost was handling, not sailing. Loading by hand ran around \$5.83 a ton; containerised, 15.8 cents. Collapsing that cost is what made splitting production across oceans worth doing.

sources.title: The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger
sources.author: Marc Levinson

hist.modern.printing-reformation.the-fir.title: The first thing that ever went viral
hist.modern.printing-reformation.the-fir.hook: Luther was not the first to attack indulgences. He was the first to do it where there was a printing press.
hist.modern.printing-reformation.the-fir.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Melanchthon's account dated to 1546 and flagged as second-hand (he reached Wittenberg in 1518). Rubin's result quoted as 'at minimum' 29 points, the abstract's wording.

hist.modern.printing-reformation.the-fir.body:
Jan Hus said most of it a century earlier and was burned at Constance in 1415. Martin Luther posted his ninety-five theses on 31 October 1517 — the nailing to the church door is a later embellishment, reported in 1546 by Melanchthon, who did not reach Wittenberg until 1518 — and within weeks the text was in print across the German lands, in Latin and then in German.

The machinery mattered more than the argument. Luther wrote short, cheap, furious pamphlets in the vernacular, and printers, who were businesses, discovered he sold. A trade built on slow Latin bibles became a news industry.

You can test this rather than assert it. Jared Rubin, in 2014, compared German-speaking cities by whether they had a press by 1500, using distance from Mainz — Gutenberg's town — as the instrument. Cities with a press by 1500 were, in Rubin's words, at minimum 29 percentage points more likely to be Protestant by 1600.

The lesson generalises uncomfortably. An idea's spread is not determined only by its truth or its appeal, but by whether the reproduction technology of the moment happens to favour its format.

recall.question: What does Rubin's use of distance from Mainz accomplish in the printing-and-Protestantism study?

options.text: It measures how far Lutheran preachers had to travel
options.why: the instrument is about presses, not preachers.

options.text: It supplies variation in press adoption
options.why: variation plausibly unrelated to a city's religious leanings, so presses can be read as a cause.

options.text: It controls for city size
options.why: size is a covariate in the regression, not what the distance instrument is for.

sources.title: Printing and Protestants: An Empirical Test of the Role of Printing in the Reformation
sources.author: Jared Rubin

hist.modern.scientific-revolution.there-.title: There was no such thing, and this is a book about it
hist.modern.scientific-revolution.there-.hook: The best-known book on the Scientific Revolution opens by denying that it happened.
hist.modern.scientific-revolution.there-.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Quote confirmed verbatim. The publisher page serves the second edition, so the source now names it; the body keeps 1996 for the first.

hist.modern.scientific-revolution.there-.body:
> "There was no such thing as the Scientific Revolution, and this is a book about it."

Steven Shapin, opening *The Scientific Revolution* (University of Chicago Press, 1996). He is not denying Kepler, Galileo, Boyle or Newton. He is refusing a label that bundles unlike people into one movement with one method — a period name coined long afterwards.

It bites because every field keeps one. The Enlightenment. The Industrial Revolution. The AI revolution. Convenient containers that hide how accidental the contents were.

sources.title: The Scientific Revolution (2nd edition; first published 1996)
sources.author: Steven Shapin

hist.science.measurement-metric.the-metr.title: The metre is 0.2 millimetres wrong, and he knew
hist.science.measurement-metric.the-metr.hook: It was meant to be one ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance. It is 0.2 mm off, and the man who knew never said.
hist.science.measurement-metric.the-metr.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Arcs corrected: Delambre took Dunkirk-Rodez, Mechain Rodez-Barcelona. Cause of death softened to 'a fever, usually identified as yellow fever'. The 0.197 mm and its cause verified as written.

hist.science.measurement-metric.the-metr.body:
In 1791 revolutionary France decided the new unit of length should belong to nobody: one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. Two astronomers were sent to measure it. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the northern arc, Dunkirk down to Rodez; Pierre Méchain took the southern, Rodez to Barcelona. Both worked through a country at war, arrested repeatedly as suspected spies, carrying instruments that looked exactly like a spy's.

Seven years later Méchain had a problem. His two sets of latitude readings at Barcelona disagreed by more than his instruments should allow. He did not report it. He revised, withheld, agonised, and went back to Spain to fix the arc, where he died in September 1804 of a fever, usually identified as yellow fever.

The metre that came out of the survey is about 0.197 mm shorter than the definition it was chasing, mostly because the survey ignored the deflection of the vertical at its southern end — a gravitational quirk, not Méchain's carelessness. His secret was a real error hiding inside a systematic one.

recall.question: Why is the metre not exactly one ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance?
recall.answer: The 1792-99 meridian survey carried a small systematic error, chiefly from ignoring the deflection of the vertical near its southern end, leaving the metre about 0.197 mm short. The unit was kept anyway, and later redefined against a bar, then a wavelength, then the speed of light.
